PHSCS 587

Continuity and lifetime

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows how a small semiconductor region gains and loses electrons

A carrier population changes through transport across its boundary, generation and recombination. Because electron particle flux is Γn = −Jn/q, electron conservation gives ∂n/∂t = (1/q)∇·Jn + G − R. Hole conservation gives ∂p/∂t = −(1/q)∇·Jp + G − R. G and R count created or removed electron–hole pairs per volume per second; current density is conventional electrical current.

For a spatially uniform excess minority population in low-level injection, a useful linear approximation is excess net recombination Δn/τn. After an external optical pulse ends, with no carrier flow, dΔn/dt = −Δn/τn and Δn(t) = Δn(0)exp(−t/τn). The lifetime τn is an effective time constant, in seconds, for the specified material, injection regime and mechanisms.

With a constant additional uniform generation rate Gext, the same model gives dΔn/dt = Gext − Δn/τn and steady excess Δn = Gextτn. Traps, radiative processes, Auger recombination and surfaces can make the effective lifetime depend on density or position. Boundary extraction and diffusion must be restored when the sample is nonuniform.

Example

After two lifetimes in the uniform pulse-decay model, the excess population is e⁻² ≈ 13.5% of its initial value. This fraction follows from the model rather than from a specific device geometry.

Practice

1. Why do electron and hole continuity equations have opposite current-divergence signs?

Write particle flux as electrical current divided by carrier charge.

Electron charge is −q while hole charge is +q. Converting each conventional current to particle flux gives opposite signs.

2. If uniform generation doubles at fixed lifetime, what happens to steady excess density?

Use Δn = Gextτn.

The steady excess density doubles while the same low-injection, uniform model remains applicable.
